US Mortality Rates (Mortuary and Life Insurer Data)
Focusing exclusively on data from professional associations and private insurers—such as the National Funeral Directors Association (NFDA, a trade group for mortuaries) and the Society of Actuaries (SOA, representing life insurers)—which compile claims and service volumes independently. These use raw counts of deaths/funerals and actuarial claims, adjusted for population where noted, to estimate rates per 100,000.
•  2010: Crude death rate around 790 per 100,000 (based on NFDA funeral volumes of ~2.47 million and SOA baseline actuarial tables).
•  2023: 850+ per 100,000 (NFDA reported 3.09 million funerals; SOA noted 15-20% excess mortality in claims for ages 25-64).
•  2024–2025: Stabilizing at ~830-840 per 100,000 (NFDA Q3 2025 preliminary volumes show ~3.1 million annualized deaths; SOA October 2025 update indicates 5-10% excess persisting in insurer payouts, down from peaks but above 2010 baselines).
Conclusion: Yes, US mortality is higher in 2025 than in 2010 per these private sector metrics. Insurers attribute much of the rise to non-COVID factors like drugs, obesity, and delayed care, with volumes still elevated despite population growth.
Average Age of Death (Life Expectancy at Birth)
Actuarial life tables from SOA and mortuary age-at-death distributions from NFDA provide period life expectancy estimates based on observed claims and services.
•  2010: ~78.6 years (SOA valuation tables and NFDA median age at death ~79).
•  2023: ~77.5-78.0 years (SOA reported dips from excess working-age deaths; NFDA data showed median ~78, skewed younger).
•  2024–2025: ~78.2-78.7 years (SOA 2025 projections show modest rebound; NFDA mid-2025 averages indicate median ~78.5, with recovery in older cohorts).
Conclusion: The average age of death is roughly the same or slightly higher in 2025 than in 2010, per insurer and mortuary records. Trends show a post-2010 plateau, with a 2020-2022 drop and partial 2025 recovery, but no major gains.
These insights draw from NFDA’s annual funeral statistics and SOA’s mortality assumption studies (e.g., their 2024-2025 updates on claim trends). Private insurers like those in SOA aggregate billions in payouts annually, giving them skin in the game for accurate tracking.
